The planned mechanics: how panels are held together, joined to each other and hung. Conceptual until modelled; finished parts move to the design reference.

FitClipShapesFree edgesBuild orderCAD
1 · How it fits together

The planned panel and cluster mechanics

Planned in decisions 0012–0014 and accepted by the user on 2026-11-21; the parts get modelled in SolidCraft next (mechanical/solidcraft/). Inside a panel, the six edge boards are sandwiched between the frame's groove at the top and the back plate's tabs at the bottom. Between panels, a rigid bridge clip holds them together: straight-sided keys on the clip sit in grooves in both back plates and carry the pull between panels, while small snaps only keep the clip on. The clip sets the seam width exactly; the bridge springs only make contact. A few panels hold the whole cluster on the wall with Dual Lock.

−2.0 → 7.0Bridge PCB, standing in the seam.
−1.3 → 1.2Clip-recess ceiling and the clip's top face (3.0 mm clip base); the clip's straight-sided keys rise 2.5 mm into grooves, up to z 1.2.
0 → 13.5Edge boards, a soldered ring of six.
3.5Spring contact point on the pads (no vias below 5.3).
5.0 → 6.6Controller board, its top flush with the floor.

7.4 → 12.2LEDs.

2 · The bridge clip

Snap-fit, no screws, no play

Same principle as Nanoleaf's linkers: something rigid sitting in slots in both panels takes the pull, and a light snap only keeps it in. Here the rigid part is a pair of straight-sided keys (chamfered at the top for lead-in) in back-plate grooves; the snap teeth in the lug windows keep the clip on and come free with a small screwdriver. The clip goes on from the back, because the bridge springs must slide onto the pads from the wall edge.

Corrected on 2026-11-21: the first version located the panels only through the snap arms, which pushed the panels apart and let them slide off the teeth. The keys fix that.

Printing: the back plate prints floor-down (lugs pointing up) and the clip prints bottom-down. The tooth and window latch faces slope about 25° from horizontal, so nothing needs support trapped inside the part (rule: overhangs up to 70°; steeper only with support standing on the bed). Keys are straight-sided, not tapered, so a pull between panels never pushes the clip off (a taper would, especially with only one panel attached). Zero play comes from a close key-in-groove fit, tuned on a test print.

4 · Free edges

Covering the pads on the outside of a cluster

5 · Build order

From a ring of boards to a cluster on the wall

  1. Ring: solder the six edge boards into a ring, with the frame as the jig.
  2. Controller: solder it at 90° to the code-0 board and seat it in the back-plate pocket.
  3. Close the panel: snap the back plate into the frame's legs, then fit the film and the bezel (no riser).
  4. Join panels: lay the panels face down, set each bridge in its clip and push the clip onto the seam until all four teeth click. Fit edge covers on free edges.
  5. Hang: press the finished cluster onto Dual Lock pads on the wall. To add a panel later, take the cluster down first (accepted by the user).

Still to design: the injection bridge's fuse relief and supply-wire exit through its clip, and how the bridge is held in the slot (snug fit or glue). Soldering and assembly jigs are roadmap item 2.3.

The code on the chips: each panel's CH32V203 node firmware, its bootloader, and the ESP32 cluster controllers that run each CAN bus.

PartsNode firmwareCAN protocolDiscovery roundRenderingTime syncUpdatesControllerPower modesGapsProduct

The pieces

Node firmwareThe application on each panel's CH32V203: CAN, discovery, effect VM, LED driver.
BootloaderA small, never-updated program that installs new node firmware over CAN.
Effect VMA tiny sandboxed interpreter that runs effect bytecode once per LED per frame.
Effect descriptorA few bytes naming an effect, its parameters, palette and start time.
SYNC / LATCHClock-sync messages, and the shared moment every panel shows a new frame.
Controller firmwareESP-IDF application on each cluster controller: CAN gateway, Wi-Fi, orchestration.
1 · Node firmware

One small program per panel

Each panel runs the same firmware. It listens on CAN, takes part in discovery, evaluates the current effect for its 12–18 LEDs, and pushes colours out on the shared latch time. Everything is interrupt- and DMA-driven, so the CPU spends most of its time asleep or idle.

LED driver

SPI1 with DMA generates the SK6812 bit timing on PA7 straight from the frame buffer, and an AHCT level shifter lifts it to the LEDs' 5 V logic. Each RGBW LED takes 32 bits, so sending 18 LEDs takes about 0.7 ms and almost no CPU.

The chain's end loops back to PA0 through a 2.2 kΩ / 3.3 kΩ divider (PA0 is not 5 V tolerant), where TIM2 counts the returned bits. Sending extra colour data and counting what returns (32 bits per LED) gives the LED count, the panel's edge count, and the position of any break. There is no backup data line, so a dead LED cuts the chain at that point.

Frame builder

Applies gamma, temporal dithering for smooth low-level fades, the per-panel brightness cap from the power budget, a flash limiter that caps how fast brightness may change, and splits each colour into RGB plus white for the RGBW LEDs.

2 · CAN protocol

Message classes, ordered by priority

Messages use 29-bit CAN IDs with the priority and class in the top bits, so bus arbitration always favours sync over bulk data. The target address or group sits in the low bits, so each node's hardware filters drop traffic that isn't for it. An 8 MHz crystal gives the clock accuracy CAN bit timing needs. CAN frames carry 8 bytes, so effect bytecode and firmware images are sent in numbered fragments.

ClassPriorityDirectionRateContents
SYNC / LATCH1 (highest)controller → allSYNC 10 Hz; LATCH per frametimestamp; frame number
Discovery2bothduring discoveryDRIVE command; SENSE report (edge code, voltage)
Effect descriptor3controller → all or a groupon changeeffect slot, parameters, palette, t₀
Stream samples4controller → node≤ 20 Hzone RGBW colour (4 bytes) per edge for simulated effects
Config5controller → noderareaddress, shape, termination, brightness cap
Node status6node → controller1 Hzsupply voltage, temperature, errors, firmware version
Bootloader7 (lowest)bothduring updatesimage chunks, CRC, acknowledgements

A proposal for the protocol document in firmware/common/protocol/.

3 · Discovery round

How the controller maps a whole cluster

Before discovery, the controller enumerates nodes: each node bids with its 96-bit chip ID using CAN arbitration, the lowest ID wins and gets a short address, and the round repeats until no one is left. The ID circuit on the Hardware page does the sensing.

The cluster controller gives every panel a turn. After one round it has the complete map: which edge of every panel faces which edge of its neighbour, regardless of how each panel was rotated when it was mounted.

4 · Rendering

The bus carries a recipe, not pixels

Every node knows where each of its LEDs sits in room coordinates. The coordinator broadcasts one short effect description and a shared clock, and every node evaluates it locally. Streaming raw RGBW colour to one 20-panel cluster (360 LEDs) at 30 fps would need about 350 kbps of payload, more than a 250 kbps CAN bus delivers after overhead. The recipe is a few bytes.

Effect VM

  • Stack-based bytecode, Q16.16 fixed point; no FPU needed.
  • Inputs: time, the LED's room position, path distance and gradient to named anchors, parameters, a random seed.
  • Operations: arithmetic, sine and noise lookups, clamp, mix, palette lookup.
  • Verified when loaded: bounded stack and loops, no memory access outside its sandbox, and an instruction budget per LED.

Budget

18 LEDs × 60 fps × 200 instructions is about 0.2 million instructions per second, a small fraction of a 144 MHz core. The same VM source is compiled to WebAssembly for the studio preview, so previews match the panels exactly.

5 · Time sync

Every panel changes on the same frame

The controller broadcasts SYNC with its clock about ten times a second, timestamped by the CAN hardware at start-of-frame. Each node trims its local clock to match. A node may finish computing a frame early or late, but it holds the result until the shared LATCH time.

6 · Updates

Updating every panel at once

  1. The controller announces an image: version, size, CRC or signature.
  2. Nodes that need it acknowledge.
  3. The controller broadcasts the chunks once to all of them at the same time; nodes request any chunks they missed.
  4. Each node checks the image, writes it, and reboots.
  5. The bootloader checks again before starting the app.

A 40 KB image broadcast over a 250 kbps bus takes a few seconds, whether the cluster has 5 panels or 50.

7 · Controller

ESP32 cluster controller firmware

Built on ESP-IDF (FreeRTOS). One controller owns each cluster's CAN bus and is the cluster's link to the coordinator.

  • CAN gateway on the built-in TWAI controller.
  • Coordinator link over Wi-Fi: effects and samples down, topology and status up.
  • Discovery: enumeration, turn scheduling, building the cluster map.
  • Time-sync relay: coordinator clock in, CAN SYNC out.
  • Termination manager: enables the far-end terminator once the topology is known.
  • Power budget: sets per-panel brightness caps so each domain stays within its supply.
  • Updates: stores node images and runs broadcast updates; updates itself with ESP-IDF's two-partition OTA.
  • Setup and offline mode: Wi-Fi setup over Bluetooth from the phone app; keeps playing the last scene, and a button cycles scenes, if the coordinator is unreachable.
8 · Power modes

From full brightness to nearly off

ModeNode MCUCAN transceiverLED railWakes on
Activerunningonon—
Idle (lights dark, ready)sleeping between framesononany message
Standbydeep sleepstandbyoffCAN bus activity
Offunpoweredunpoweredoffsupply switched on

Standby is what brings idle draw down from about 0.3–0.5 W per panel. The CAN transceiver's standby pin is on a GPIO, and a P-MOSFET switches the LED rail off; the 24 → 5 V buck stays on for the MCU and CAN.

9 · Gaps

What the firmware plan is still missing

Tier A

Needs hardware support: settle before the schematic

Sleep and wake

Idle draw of 0.3–0.5 W per panel comes mostly from the MCU and CAN transceiver. Rev A has the transceiver's Rs pin on a GPIO (standby keeps the receiver on, so it can wake on bus traffic), and a P-MOSFET on the controller board now switches the LED rail (the 24 → 5 V buck stays on).

Next step: Write and measure the sleep sequence: on an OFF broadcast, buck off, MCU deep sleep, transceiver standby; wake on any bus activity.

Diagnostics

Installed panels are hard to inspect. Each node should report supply voltage, temperature, CAN error counters and LED chain health. Supply voltage needs a resistor divider on a spare ADC pin.

Next step: Add the divider footprint. The apps then show a voltage-drop and fault map of every wall.

Bootloader safety

A power cut during an update must never brick a panel inside a wall. The bootloader has to be immutable, check a CRC or signature before starting the app, and stay in update mode if the app is invalid. That needs flash headroom.

Next step: The CH32V203F6P6 has 224 KB of flash, of which only the first 32 KB runs without wait states. Keep the bootloader (about 8 KB) and hot code there, and the effect slots further up.

Tier B

Design before writing code

Enumeration and addressing

Nodes start with only a 96-bit chip ID. The controller needs a collision-free way to find them on a shared bus and hand out short addresses.

Next step: Use CAN arbitration on the chip ID (lowest ID wins, repeat until none are left) and store the address in flash so it survives reboots.

Time sync accuracy

Effects that cross walls and rooms only look continuous if every cluster agrees on time.

Next step: Timestamp SYNC frames in hardware at start-of-frame. Target ≤ 0.1 ms within a cluster and ≤ 2 ms across clusters, and measure it with a photodiode on two panels.

Discovery robustness

LED PWM currents add noise on GND, and a half-seated bridge reads between valid codes.

Next step: Discover with LEDs off, average many samples, reject between-band readings, and re-run when the node count changes.

Write the CAN protocol down

Message IDs, enumeration, discovery, time sync, frame latch, effect descriptors and the bootloader are shared by nodes and controllers.

Next step: Keep it in firmware/common/protocol/.

Tier C

Planning

Firmware lockstep

Every node in a cluster must run a compatible effect library.

Next step: Add a version handshake; the controller refuses effects on mismatched nodes.

Provisioning and OTA

Several controllers need Wi-Fi setup, and both controllers and nodes need safe updates.

Next step: Signed updates with rollback.

10 · Product

Firmware for a product

  • Signed firmware for nodes and controllers, with secure boot on the ESP32.
  • Staged rollouts, automatic rollback on the controller, and a fail-safe bootloader on the nodes.
  • No default passwords, a vulnerability disclosure policy, and a stated support period (UK PSTI and the EU Cyber Resilience Act).
  • Fault logs that support staff can read remotely, with the owner's consent.

Everything above the controllers: the coordinator, the room model and voxel effects, the phone and desktop apps, and how people create and share effects.

PartsArchitectureAR placementBetween roomsCreating effectsPublishingAppsIntegrationsGapsProduct

The pieces

CoordinatorThe always-on service that holds the room model and runs effects for the whole home.
Room modelClusters, panels, walls, doors and a voxel grid, all in one building frame in metres.
AnchorA named place in the room model (floor, ceiling, a doorway, a room centre) that effects refer to.
EffectA recipe for light over space and time, written against the room rather than a layout.
Effect packageA signed .lfx bundle: manifest, bytecode or script, parameters and a preview.
StudioThe desktop editor for building, previewing and publishing effects.
Phone appSetup, AR placement and everyday control.
GalleryAn optional online library for sharing and installing effects.
1 · Architecture

One coordinator, three kinds of client

The coordinator is the only always-on software. It keeps the room model, compiles and checks effects, runs stateful simulations, and talks to every cluster controller. The phone app, the desktop studio and home automation are all clients of its API.

2 · Room placement

How the phone finds every panel in 3D

Discovery already gives the exact shape of each cluster, but not where it sits in the room. The AR app supplies that. The coordinator makes every panel flash a unique colour sequence at the same time, on the shared clock. The phone watches through ARKit, which knows its own position and which way is down on every camera frame.

Why a cluster only needs a few panels seen

  • Discovery already gives the panel positions inside each cluster, in millimetres.
  • Three or more decoded panels fix the cluster's 6-DoF pose. Extra panels give a least-squares fit, and a large residual flags a misread code.
  • ARKit's world frame is gravity-aligned and metric, so "down" and scale come for free.
  • Moving a cluster later means re-scanning only that cluster.

Joining rooms into one frame

  • One walk-through: scan room to room in one session. ARKit keeps a single world frame, with small drift that grows with distance.
  • Per-room scans: save each room's ARWorldMap and join rooms through a shared anchor seen from both sides, such as a cluster visible through the doorway or a marker on the door frame.
  • RoomPlan (LiDAR iPhones) returns walls, doors and openings. These become the walls and portals of the voxel model in the next section.
  • Output: one building frame in metres, stored in the Room Layout JSON.

Flash safety: codes run at about 4 symbols per second at low brightness, using colour steps of similar brightness rather than bright on/off flashes. See Gaps.

3 · Between rooms

Voxels let effects travel the way a person would

If effects used plain straight-line distance, a ripple starting in room A would light the far side of the shared wall almost immediately, as if the wall weren't there. The coordinator keeps a sparse voxel model of the building, built from RoomPlan walls and doors. It computes distance through free space, so wavefronts bend through doorways and reach the next room in the right order.

Field effects run on the nodes

Waves, gradients and ripples are formulas. For building-scale effects the coordinator precomputes each panel's path distance from a few named sources (front door, each room's centre) and sends it once: a value at the panel centre plus a gradient across the panel. Nodes then evaluate colour = f(distance − speed × t) locally, with no ongoing traffic.

Simulated effects run on the coordinator

Smoke, fire, particles bouncing off walls and flocks moving between rooms need state, so the coordinator simulates them on the voxel grid and sends low-resolution samples: one colour per edge, about 20 times a second. 100 hexagons × 6 edges × 4 bytes (RGBW) × 20 Hz is about 385 kbps in total, spread across ~10 clusters, or about 40 kbps per CAN bus.

4 · Creating effects

Three ways to make an effect

Every effect is written against the room, not against a particular layout. It refers to anchors (floor, ceiling, walls, doorways, room centres, named points) and to path distance through the building, so one effect runs in any home.

Presets

Pick a built-in effect, set its sliders and palette, choose which rooms or surfaces it covers, and save it as a scene. No code.

Visual graph

Wire blocks together: inputs (time, position, distance from an anchor, path distance, audio level, noise), maths (sine, mix, clamp) and colour (palette, hue shift). The graph compiles to node bytecode and previews live on your room.

Script

For stateful effects (particles, smoke, games, reactions to events) a sandboxed script runs on the coordinator with access to the voxel grid, panels and events such as a door sensor or a music beat. It streams samples to the panels.

  • White channel: effects can set the white LED directly for clean whites, pastels and warm light, or let the panels derive it from RGB.
  • Scenes and timelines: sequence effects with transitions, and trigger them by time, sunrise or sunset, or events.
  • Preview: on your scanned room, or on sample rooms to check that an effect travels well before sharing it.

From the editor to someone else's wall

Gallery

  • Browse by room type, mood and motion level, with preview clips.
  • Install in one tap from the phone or the studio; packages can also be shared as files.
  • Versions and remixes keep a record of where an effect came from.
  • Licence choice at publish time; reports and takedowns for problems.
  • Packages are signed by their author and re-checked locally on install.
6 · Apps

Phone and desktop

Phone app

  • Guided setup: Wi-Fi for each controller over Bluetooth, then a live discovery view.
  • AR scan and placement, room by room.
  • Point the camera at a panel to identify it, or tap one to make it blink.
  • Everyday control: scenes, brightness, colour, per room.
  • Gallery browsing and installs; a fault map with voltage drop and offline panels.

Desktop studio

  • 3D room view with a live preview that runs the real effect VM.
  • Graph editor and script editor with instant reload.
  • Timeline for scenes and transitions.
  • Publishing, device management, firmware updates and logs.

Suggested stack

  • One web UI served by the coordinator, used by both the desktop and the phone apps.
  • Native AR modules only: Swift with ARKit and RoomPlan on iPhone, Kotlin with ARCore on Android.
  • The node effect VM in portable C, built for the CH32V203 and for WebAssembly.
7 · Integrations

Fitting into the rest of the home

  • Home Assistant: a local integration or MQTT discovery, exposing rooms, scenes and effects.
  • Matter: a bridge exposing each room or cluster as a light (on/off, brightness, colour).
  • Schedules: sunrise, sunset and circadian colour temperature.
  • Events: a motion or door sensor can start a ripple from that doorway.
  • Audio-reactive: levels from a phone, desktop microphone or line-in, streamed to the coordinator.
  • Screen sync: the desktop app samples the screen edges and streams colours to nearby clusters.
8 · Gaps

What the software plan is still missing

Tier A

Platform decisions

AR app platform

iPhone Safari has no WebXR AR, so an iPhone needs a native ARKit app (a Mac with Xcode). RoomPlan needs a LiDAR iPhone. Android ARCore is easier.

Next step: Pick the scanning phone. Build a manual-placement fallback in the coordinator UI.

Local-first vs. cloud

Accounts, remote access and the gallery need a server. Nothing else should.

Next step: Run all control on the coordinator. Make the gallery optional, and allow installing an effect from a file.

Tier B

Design before building

Flash safety

AR codes and some effects flash. Rapid high-contrast or saturated-red flashing can trigger photosensitive seizures.

Next step: Keep AR codes at low brightness with near-equal-luminance colour steps, at most about 3 changes per second. Cap flash rates in the effect engine and add a calm mode.

Gallery trust and moderation

Published effects come from strangers. A careless or malicious effect could flash dangerously or exhaust node resources.

Next step: Sign packages, re-run the safety and budget checks on install, keep effects sandboxed with no network or file access, and support reports and takedowns.

Effect portability

An effect written in one home has to work in another with different rooms and layouts.

Next step: Write effects against anchors and path distance, with fallbacks when an anchor is missing. Preview on sample rooms before publishing.

Tier C

Planning

Build the simulator first

Layouts, discovery, the CAN protocol and effects can all be developed before hardware exists.

Next step: The simulator later becomes the coordinator UI's preview.

Coordinator choices

The host (Pi or ESP32), integrations (Home Assistant, MQTT) and effect authoring (built-in library or scripting) are undecided.

Next step: Decide alongside the simulator work.

  • Bridges are cheap now. The seam bridge uses $0.02 springs, so a bridge costs about $0.70–1.20 instead of $3.40–7.15 with Harwin springs. What's left is spread across the edge PCBs, LEDs, the controller board and bridges.

13 · Compared with Nanoleaf

Parts cost and brightness against Nanoleaf

Our numbers are parts cost for a personal build; Nanoleaf's are retail kit prices, which include a controller, power supply, app, warranty and support. On parts alone we come in at roughly half to the same price per m², and likely 2–3× cheaper per unit of light, because 12–18 full-size LEDs per panel put out more raw light than Nanoleaf's 1–2 W panels. Our brightness is an estimate until the optics test measures it.

Price per 100 lm≈$3–36 (mid ≈$10)≈$21–29≈$25–33

Why our brightness range is wide

  • No full-white lumen rating exists for the SKC6812RGBW. Its white channel is rated about 2.5 cd (roughly 8 lm), and vendor claims for similar 5050 chips are about 20 lm per LED. The estimate uses 8–20 lm per LED.
  • Edge lighting through diffuser film loses light; the estimate assumes 50–70% gets out.
  • Nanoleaf gets more light per watt (≈50 lm/W against our rough 15–60 lm/W); the RGBW white channel narrows the gap compared with mixing white from RGB.

What our numbers leave out

  • Shipping and import duties, often 15–40% more.
  • Assembly time, printer hours, prototypes and spares.
  • The risk of a first-generation design, against a finished product with an app, warranty and support.

Nanoleaf prices vary by region and date. Sources: Best Buy (Shapes kit), Tech Advisor, Crutchfield, Adorama (Canvas kit), JB Hi-Fi, MobileSyrup, Superlighting (5050 lumens claim), Superlighting (WS2815 power).

14 · Gaps

What the hardware plan is still missing

Ordered by how much damage each does if it is found late. Tier A items get a cheap prototype before any custom boards are ordered.

Tier A

Could force a redesign: prototype before ordering custom boards

Optics are unproven

With only 2–3 LEDs per edge shining across an air gap, a thin diffuser film is likely to show a bright spot near each LED and a dimmer centre. Film spreads light less than thick opal acrylic. Panel depth, LED aim, back reflectance and film choice are all open.

Next step: A test box with a 100 mm-edge hexagon and cut 5 V SK6812 RGBW strip: 15 / 25 / 35 mm depth, white matte vs. foil back, LEDs aimed across vs. at the back, and one vs. two film layers.

Seam bridge and carrier

The bridge is a thin PCB standing in the seam, with 20 low-cost LCSC top-contact springs (BW0019 series, ≈$0.02) pressing on pads on each panel's exterior face, held by a printed carrier. Unproven: the springs' current rating and force (not yet confirmed from the datasheet), whether a panel slides in without snagging them, seam width, carrier retention, and tolerance to a few mm of wall unevenness.

Next step: Prototype the bridge and carrier. Measure contact resistance, current per spring, insertion and seam width. The Harwin flat bridge (decision 0001) is the fallback.

Corner joints are a large hand job

100 hexagons need about 4,800 corner joints. The pads are all SMD now (signals on the inward face, power on the exterior face), but they are still joined by hand with solder beads and a bent strap across each outside corner. With 100 mm panels a wall needs about 2.25× as many panels as with 150 mm ones, so the joint count per wall goes up too. Corner angles differ by shape, and each board needs its own ID resistor.

Next step: Cut the nets that cross corners, use solder-bead castellations or a corner jumper PCB per shape, and panelize a "hex kit" with ID codes 0–5 pre-assembled.

Standby power

With only 12–18 LEDs per panel, idle draw is now mostly the MCU and CAN transceiver: about 0.3–0.5 W per panel, or 30–50 W for 100 panels with the lights off.

Next step: Sleep the MCU, put the CAN transceiver in standby with wake on bus activity, and switch the LED rail off with the controller board's P-MOSFET; or switch whole domains off at the supply.

Printing logistics

Bed size is solved: a 100 mm-edge hexagon is 200 mm across its corners and fits common 220–256 mm beds in one piece. Print time is still large, roughly 1–2 h per panel, or 100–450 printer-hours for 100–225 panels. PETG is not flame-retardant.

Next step: Print several frames per plate and budget the printer time.

Mounting, especially ceilings

The spec has no mounting method. Ceiling panels need positive retention, walls are not flat, and a panel in the middle of a cluster must be removable for repair.

Next step: Design a mounting plate that also takes the bridge insertion force.

Tier B

Decide before schematic capture

Panel shape: auto-detect or setting

One firmware image serves every shape. The last LED's data output loops back to the MCU, so firmware can count its own LEDs and work out the edge count; a stored setting is the alternative. No strap resistor.

Next step: Route the last LED's output back to a 5 V-tolerant timer-capture pin through a series resistor. Later, decide whether auto-detect or the stored setting is primary.

Exposed contacts need protection

Bare pads get touched (ESD), hot-plugging charges the LED and bulk capacitors through the springs, and a board sliding in can briefly touch the wrong spring.

Next step: Staggered pad heights (GND first) stay. Decision 0011 makes every bus line survive a sustained 24 V short: TCAN1044V (±58 V), NUP3105 CAN TVS, 10 k SENSE resistor, open-drain DRIVE through 470 Ω, TLV431 3V3 clamp, and a per-panel PTC. Verify on the prototype.

CAN loops and termination

Three hexagons meeting at a vertex close a loop in the bus, and the electrically farthest node isn't known until after discovery.

Next step: Run a 10–20 node loop test at 125 / 250 / 500 kbps. Consider MCU-switchable split termination.

RGBW dim levels and flicker

RGBW is decided (SKC6812RGBW, neutral white). Still open: 8-bit PWM bands at night-time brightness, and the PWM frequency for camera and phone flicker.

Next step: Plan temporal dithering in node firmware. Measure low-level dimming and flicker in the optics test.

Programming and test

100+ MCUs need a first flash, and every board should be tested before it is glued into a panel.

Next step: SWD pads, a pogo-pin jig with a WCH-LinkE, an LED and ID test fixture, and about 5% spare boards.

Missing target numbers

Brightness, maximum power per panel, board height (panel depth), contact-pad position, weight, frame rate, latency, maximum cluster size and boot time are all unset.

Next step: Set them once the optics test is done.

Tier C

Planning

Phasing

Ordering 100+ panels before the risky parts are proven wastes money.

Next step: Phase 0 prototypes (optics, bridge, corners, CAN loops), then one bench kit, a 5–10 panel cluster, multi-cluster with AR, and only then volume.

15 · Product

What it would take to sell this: hardware and business

The personal-build design works as a prototype for a product, but a product changes the economics and the paperwork. The core problem is price: comparable modular panel kits sell for very roughly $15–25 per panel, and retail is typically 3–4× the landed cost of materials. That puts the target material cost near $5–8 per hexagon, against about $9–18 today. The gap is spread across the fixed per-panel parts: edge PCBs, the controller board, LEDs and bridges.

$9–18material cost per hexagon now
≈$5–8target material cost for retail pricing
$15–60kmoulding tooling per part family (rough)
$15–40kcertification testing, one-time (rough)

Hardware changes from personal build to product

AreaPersonal buildProduct
Enclosure3D-printed PETGInjection-moulded PC or PC/ABS rated UL94 V-0. Tooling is roughly $15–60k per part family.
AssemblyHand-soldered corner jointsNo hand soldering: a one-piece ring PCB, board-to-board connectors, or a moulded frame that captures the boards.
DiffuserLCD-style diffuser film in a printed frameFilm held in a moulded frame, or a moulded diffuser.
Panel connectionsSeam bridge PCB with $0.02 LCSC springs in a printed carrierSame approach with a moulded carrier and springs qualified for mating cycles.
Power24 V bench supplies, user-wiredListed plug-in adapters. In the US, Class 2 limits each circuit to about 100 W, so domains are sized to that.
Standby≈0.3–0.5 W per panel idleEU standby limits (roughly 0.5 W, or about 2 W networked) apply to the product, so per-panel sleep and supply gating are required.
LED count2–3 per edgeSame, once the optics test confirms it.

Certification and compliance

RequirementApplies toWhat it means here
FCC Part 15B (US)Panels and controllerUnintentional emissions. Fast LED data edges and CAN must pass.
FCC 15C / EU RED (radio)ControllerUse a pre-certified ESP32 module so the product inherits its radio grant.
CE: EMC, RED, RoHS, REACH, WEEE (EU)Whole systemDeclaration of conformity and a technical file. 24 V is below the Low Voltage Directive, but the adapter is not.
UL / ETL safety listingPanels and supplyMost retailers require it. Flame-rated plastics and a listed supply.
IEC 62471 photobiological safetyPanelsBlue-light hazard classification.
Energy rulesSystem and adapterEU Ecodesign standby and networked standby; US DoE adapter efficiency.
CybersecurityController and appUK PSTI (in force), EU Cyber Resilience Act (phasing in), US Cyber Trust Mark (voluntary). No default passwords, a disclosure policy, secure updates.
Matter (optional)ControllerExpected by smart-home buyers. Alliance membership and test fees apply.

A starting map, not legal advice. Confirm scope with a test lab before design freeze. Firmware and software obligations are on their own pages.

Reliability testing

  • Connector mating cycles and contact resistance over life.
  • Thermal cycling at full white in a closed panel.
  • LED failure rate against the warranty period.
  • Mounting on painted drywall, plaster, tile and textured walls; ceiling pull-out force.
  • Shipping drop tests and packaging.

Business and legal

  • Patent freedom-to-operate search before any investment. Established brands hold patents on connectable light panels and layout detection.
  • Trademark, company formation, product liability insurance.
  • Minimum order quantities and the cash to hold inventory.
  • Validate demand first, for example with a crowdfunding campaign.
  • Sales channels, returns handling and retailer requirements.

Where it could stand out: most current products map a layout in 2D on one surface. Room-scale effects that run continuously across walls, ceilings and rooms, placed by an AR scan, are the differentiator worth protecting and demonstrating early.
